note: Short summaries of the guidance in the pages they cite, for choosing between alternatives. They are a starting point and are NOT a substitute for the sources: open the link before relying on a row. Written from the published guidance; not re-verified line by line against the pages on the date of this snapshot.

api-type.title: HTTP API, REST API, or GraphQL (AppSync)

options.name: HTTP API
useWhen: You need a low-cost, low-latency proxy to Lambda or HTTP backends
JWT or OIDC authorization is enough
watchOut: It lacks API keys and usage plans, request validation, caching, and some WAF and private-endpoint features of REST APIs

options.name: REST API
useWhen: You need API keys and usage plans, request validation, response caching, WAF, or private endpoints
watchOut: Higher price per request than an HTTP API

options.name: GraphQL (AppSync)
useWhen: Clients need to choose their fields, combine several sources in one call, or subscribe to changes
watchOut: A different operating model: schema design, resolvers, and authorization per field are yours to manage

askFirst: Which clients call it and what do they need to authenticate with?
Is per-client throttling or an API key required?

messaging.title: SQS, SNS, or EventBridge

options.name: SQS
useWhen: One consumer group must process each message, at its own pace, with retries and a dead-letter queue
You need to buffer bursts and protect a downstream service
watchOut: Standard queues deliver at least once and possibly out of order: handlers must be idempotent
A visibility timeout shorter than the consumer's processing time causes duplicates

options.name: SNS
useWhen: One message must fan out to many subscribers (queues, functions, HTTP endpoints)
watchOut: Push delivery: pair each slow subscriber with its own queue

options.name: EventBridge
useWhen: Producers and consumers should be decoupled by event content, with routing rules, schema discovery, archive and replay, or SaaS and cross-account events
watchOut: It is an event router, not a buffer: delivery targets still need retries and a dead-letter queue
Event size and throughput quotas apply

askFirst: How many independent consumers need each message?
Does a consumer need to be able to fall behind without losing messages?
Do events need to be routed by their content?

workflow.title: Step Functions Standard or Express

options.name: Standard
useWhen: Workflows are long-running, need an audit trail of every step, or must not run a step twice
watchOut: Priced per state transition: chatty workflows get expensive

options.name: Express
useWhen: Workflows are short and run at high volume, such as event processing
watchOut: Limited duration, at-least-once semantics for asynchronous executions, and execution history only through logs

askFirst: How long can one execution take?
What happens if a step runs twice?

integration.title: Lambda or a direct service integration

options.name: Direct integration (API Gateway, EventBridge Pipes, Step Functions SDK integrations)
useWhen: The step only moves or maps data between services, with no business logic
watchOut: Mapping templates and error handling are configuration you must test and operate

options.name: Lambda
useWhen: There is logic, validation, or composition that needs code
watchOut: Every function is code to patch, monitor, and size, and adds a cold start and a timeout to reason about

askFirst: Is there any decision in this step, or only plumbing?

data-store.title: DynamoDB or a relational database

options.name: DynamoDB
useWhen: Access patterns are known up front, you need predictable single-digit-millisecond access at any scale, and no ad hoc joins
watchOut: Changing the key schema later usually means a migration; the design follows the queries

options.name: Relational (for example Aurora)
useWhen: Queries are varied or ad hoc, you need joins and transactions across entities
watchOut: Connections, scaling, and cost model differ from DynamoDB; Lambda needs connection management

askFirst: List the queries: which are known and which are not?
What consistency and transactions does the business need?

sync-async.title: Synchronous or asynchronous

options.name: Synchronous
useWhen: The caller needs the result now and can wait for it
watchOut: Timeouts and failures propagate to the caller; chains of calls multiply latency

options.name: Asynchronous
useWhen: The caller only needs an acknowledgment and the work can finish later
watchOut: You must design for duplicates, ordering, retries, dead-letter handling, and how the caller learns the outcome

askFirst: What does the caller do with the result?
What is the longest acceptable wait?
